title: Starting piano and C-melody saxophone
summary: Kmen took piano lessons, took up a C-melody saxophone around 1927 and read sheet music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: But did you play any musical instrument when you were growing up in Saratoga?
I started playing piano very early. I don't remember when. I didn't play it very well, but I played saxophone I guess from the time I was about twelve or so. I should make it 1927 or so. Late 1920s.
Did you play piano by ear?
No, I took lessons. Used to. Like a lot of kids. Did just about as well as a lot of kids.
I guess you hated taking lessons. I think.
Yes, indeed. Worse, I hated practicing.
And what inspired you to take up saxophone?

I always liked the pictures of saxophones in magazines. By this time you could hear a lot of it on the radio. I don't know who can explain these things, but I always had an affinity for the sound. I just really liked the sound of a sax or saxophones. There was an analogy too, isn't it? Yes, but it also sounded to me like much more than a novelty. I just liked the sound. I always had, so do. A good sax choir is one of my principal joys. And a fellow who was living in my house, he used to go off in periodic toots, the kind of genteel drunkards that you don't find much anymore in the country, sober for six months and then disappear for a week and come back. Boarder at the house, he came back after one of these toots with a saxophone and that was it. Where he got it, nobody knows, including him. What kind of saxophone? It was a buffet C melody. That was convenient because there were more C melodies around. You remember Trombauer played a C melody and Jack Purvis, who I believe possibly was from New Orleans, also played a C melody sax. It got a distinctive and very pretty sound on it. Jack who? Purvis. Oh, Pettis, huh?
Purvis is a trumpet player. No, Pettis, Jack Pettis.
Well, Pettis I think is from around Bungalusa. No, you're quite right.

Jack Pettis, definitely Jack Pettis. I heard his orchestra many times. He played up in Albany, New York, you know, visiting there, but that was close to my home and we could always hear the bands from Albany on the radio. You could read sheet music. You could read sheet music. This is what a lot of people did in those days. Got a whole piece of sheet music and got a whole piano player of some kind, drummer of some kind. And the C horn, you could read over your shoulder the melody line when you were in business.
No transposing, no problems. No transposing, no problems.

No transposing, no problems. That's right. And that's the way I started and apparently there was enough to be and I guess looking back, enough dances and so forth that a lot of people were willing to put up with some pretty sad music just in order to have some music. You had a good chance to pick up experience.
Did you take lessons on the same melody track?
